meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нимать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to understand', paired with 'понять'.

examples.trans: I understand.
I want to go to the sea, you know?

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to say, to tell', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: What did you say?
Excuse me, where's the metro?
Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'жалуйста').

examples.trans: A coffee, please.
Thank you! — You're welcome.
Please see him out.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'what for, why', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What have you come for?
What's that for?
Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'делать'.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
I'll do it tomorrow.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'person; (pl) people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is a good person.
There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ступать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to act, treat', paired with 'поступить'.

examples.text: Вика, так нельзя поступать со мной!
examples.trans: Vika, you cannot treat me like this!

examples.text: Я всегда стараюсь поступать честно, как он.
examples.trans: I always try to act honestly, like him.

examples.text: Я не понимаю, почему они так поступают.
examples.trans: I do not understand why they act like that.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to give; (imperative) let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.trans: Let's talk.
He gives me a book.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'house; building; home' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There's a new building on Simashko Street.
This is my home.

examples.text: Квартира будет отличная. На Симашко есть новый дом.
examples.trans: It'll be an excellent flat. There's a new building on Simashko Street.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ъяснить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to explain', paired with 'объяснять'.

examples.trans: I'll explain everything later.
Explain, please.
I will explain everything to you right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'all right, OK', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go.
OK, I'm coming.
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nobody', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Nobody will come in.
I know the town like nobody else.

examples.text: Садитесь и держите дверь. Никто не войдёт.
examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door. Nobody will come in.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.
See the markers? They're from Japan!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not a (single); neither... nor', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I haven't got a penny.
Not a word!

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'war' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Read The Art of War, by Sun Tzu!
This book tells about the war.

examples.text: В прошлый раз я думала, война началась.
examples.trans: Last time I thought a war had started.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'without', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's no problem.
This time there's no trick.
That's no problem at all.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'теря'). Common feminine noun meaning 'loss' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Москва снимет вас за потерю доверия.
examples.trans: Moscow will dismiss you for loss of confidence.

examples.text: Но Москва снимет вас за потерю доверия.
examples.trans: But Moscow will dismiss you for loss of confidence.

examples.text: Жизнь полна разных потерь и приобретений.
examples.trans: Life is full of various losses and gains.

бывать.gloss: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit

meanings.en: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit', paired with 'быть'.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.
That happens.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'our, ours', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'грамма'). Common feminine noun meaning 'programme' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What is your programme?
The programme will be on the website.
Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('interesting').

examples.trans: This is a very interesting book.
Funny you should say that!

examples.text: Такая интересная. Я тебе не бандит.
examples.trans: Funny you should say that. I'm no gangster for you.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нять'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to understand', paired with 'понимать'.

examples.trans: I didn't understand.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?
I understand you.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('big, large').

examples.trans: A big city.
The sum is very large.

examples.text: Аракелян просит время. Сумма очень большая.
examples.trans: Arakelyan is asking for more time. The sum is very large.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from; of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: A letter from Mum.
I'm tired of work.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'традать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to suffer', paired with 'пострадать'.

examples.trans: He is supposed to suffer.
People are suffering because of him.

examples.text: Ну и что? Он должен страдать, а нам нужна информация.
examples.trans: So what? He is supposed to suffer, and we need the information.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'винный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('innocent').

examples.text: Больше всего от войны страдают невинные.
examples.trans: In any war, it is the innocent who suffer the most.

examples.text: Сегодня у шефа очень невинный день в ресторане.
examples.trans: Today the chef is having a very innocent day at the restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'which, who', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Чтобы он вернул деньги, которые украл.
examples.trans: For him to give back the money he stole.

examples.text: Который ему город подарил! И откуда у Аллы Евгеньевны новая шуба!
examples.trans: Which the city donated to him! And where Alla Yevgenyevna got a new fur coat!

оказаться.gloss: to turn out to be, find oneself

meanings.en: to turn out to be, find oneself
meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to turn out to be, find oneself', paired with 'оказываться'.

examples.trans: You turned out to be ungrateful.

examples.text: Он внезапно оказался в центре событий.
examples.trans: He suddenly found himself in the center of events.
And you turned out to be an ungrateful woman!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('drawn in, involved').

examples.text: Которые оказались втянуты в сражение против своей воли.
examples.trans: Those who get dragged into the battle against their will.

examples.text: Сегодня у шефа очень втянутый день в ресторане.
examples.trans: Today the chef is having a very drawn in day at the restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ражение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'battle' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Которые оказались втянуты в сражение против своей воли.
examples.trans: Those who get dragged into the battle against their will.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новое сражение.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new battle.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'against', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm against it.
He is against the cluster.

examples.text: Все в городе хотят этот кластер. Только ты против.
examples.trans: Everyone in town wants this cluster. Only you are against it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

examples.text: А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'will; freedom, liberty' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Yes, swear on my freedom!
A real head chef requires strong willpower.

examples.text: У меня есть опыт и сильная воля.
examples.trans: I have experience and strong willpower.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'path, way, journey' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Here is a movie: A Thorny Path.

examples.text: Давай, счастливого пути и хорошей дороги!
examples.trans: Go ahead, safe travels and have a good road!

examples.text: Ты сам выбрал этот страшный путь.
examples.trans: You chose this terrible path yourself.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'deceit, trick' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It's another trick.
This time there's no trick.

examples.text: Нина, не слушай. Это опять обман.
examples.trans: Nina, don't listen. It's another trick.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'at times, occasionally, sometimes', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся в своей правоте.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize we were right.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся, что были правы.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize that we were right.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'манутый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('deceived, cheated').

examples.text: И порой обманутым оказываешься ты сам.
examples.trans: And sometimes the one who ends up deceived is yourself.

examples.text: Сегодня у шефа очень обманутый день в ресторане.
examples.trans: Today the chef is having a very deceived day at the restaurant.

оказываться.gloss: to turn out to be, prove to be

meanings.en: to turn out to be, prove to be
meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to turn out to be, prove to be', paired with 'оказаться'.

examples.trans: Simple things turn out to be important.

examples.text: Иногда простые вещи оказываются самыми важными.
examples.trans: Sometimes simple things turn out to be the most important.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself, myself, himself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, простите меня, пожалуйста. Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, please forgive me. I don't know myself how it happened.

examples.text: Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: I don't know myself how it happened.
